title: Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) Testing
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: ANA detects auto‑antibodies against nuclear components and is a key screening tool for systemic autoimmune diseases. Interpretation requires pattern, titer and clinical context, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: ANA is an indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) test that identifies IgG antibodies binding to cellular nuclei. A positive result supports a diagnosis of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease (SARD) but is not disease‑specific.
b: Positive if fluorescence at ≥1:40 on HEp‑2 cells (screening cut‑off).
Higher titers (≥1:160) increase specificity for SARD.

sections.p: Auto‑antibody production is driven by loss of tolerance. In low‑resource settings the most common ANA‑positive diseases are:
b: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) – most frequent cause of high‑titer ANA.
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) – nucleolar pattern.
Mixed connective tissue disease – speckled pattern with anti‑RNP.
Dermatomyositis – anti‑Mi‑2 pattern.
Drug‑induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide).

sections.p: Patients present with multisystem complaints that reflect immune complex deposition or vasculopathy.
b: Malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers (SLE).
Raynaud’s phenomenon, sclerodactyly, dysphagia (systemic sclerosis).
Proximal muscle weakness, Gottron papules (dermatomyositis).
Arthralgia, serositis, renal or neurologic involvement.

t.b: Is there an auto‑antibody to nuclear antigens? – Positive fluorescence confirms ANA; pattern (homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, centromere) narrows differential.
How strong is the antibody response? – Titers ≥1:160 are more likely true disease; low titers (1:40‑1:80) can be seen in healthy individuals or infections.
Is disease activity high in SLE? – Low complement supports active immune complex disease.

t.a: Specific auto‑antibodies (anti‑dsDNA, anti‑Sm, anti‑RNP, anti‑centromere, anti‑Mi‑2)
t.b: Which disease is most likely? – Anti‑dsDNA = SLE; anti‑centromere = limited systemic sclerosis; anti‑Mi‑2 = dermatomyositis.

sections.p: Unchecked autoimmune activity can lead to organ‑life‑threatening damage.
b: Lupus nephritis – rising creatinine, proteinuria, hypertension.
Pulmonary hypertension in systemic sclerosis – dyspnoea, syncope.
Myositis with respiratory failure – progressive weakness, hypoxia.
Severe vasculitis – skin necrosis, digital gangrene.

sections.p: Treat the underlying autoimmune disease; ANA itself is not therapeutic.
b: SLE – hydroxychloroquine (disease‑modifying, safe in pregnancy), low‑dose steroids for flares, add mycophenolate or azathioprine for organ involvement.
Systemic sclerosis – ACE inhibitors for renal crisis, endothelin‑receptor antagonists for pulmonary hypertension, avoid high‑dose steroids (risk of renal crisis).
Dermatomyositis – steroids plus methotrexate; avoid long‑term high‑dose steroids alone due to infection risk.
Drug‑induced lupus – stop offending drug; symptoms usually resolve.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of disease activity and treatment toxicity is essential.
b: SLE – check ANA, dsDNA, complement every 3‑6 months; urine protein each visit.
Systemic sclerosis – annual echocardiogram, pulmonary function tests, renal function.
Educate patients on sun protection, infection prophylaxis, and medication adherence.

sections.p: Other serologic tests that may be ordered in similar presentations.
b: Anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) – vasculitis, not ANA.
Rheumatoid factor – rheumatoid arthritis, can be positive in SLE but is a different target.
Anti‑phospholipid antibodies – clotting disorder, may coexist with ANA‑positive disease.

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Low‑titer ANA in healthy individuals – avoid over‑diagnosis.
False‑negative ANA if testing performed during immunosuppression.
Pattern misreading without experienced eye – may miss centromere or nucleolar patterns.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid rise in creatinine or new proteinuria (possible lupus nephritis).
Sudden dyspnoea or chest pain with known systemic sclerosis (pulmonary hypertension or pulmonary fibrosis).
Severe muscle weakness with respiratory compromise (myositis).

faq.q: Can a positive ANA alone diagnose lupus?
faq.a: No. ANA is a screening tool; diagnosis requires clinical criteria and often a disease‑specific antibody such as anti‑dsDNA.

faq.q: Why is the ANA titer important?
faq.a: Higher titers (≥1:160) increase the likelihood of true autoimmune disease, whereas low titers are common in healthy people.

faq.q: What does a nucleolar pattern suggest?
faq.a: It is most often seen in systemic sclerosis, especially the diffuse form.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with malar rash and arthritis has ANA 1:80 homogeneous. What is your next step? — Order anti‑dsDNA and complement; low‑titer ANA alone does not confirm SLE.
A patient with Raynaud’s, skin thickening and ANA 1:320 nucleolar pattern presents with new dyspnoea. What complication should you suspect? — Pulmonary hypertension; arrange echocardiogram urgently.
Why is hydroxychloroquine preferred as first‑line therapy in SLE despite a positive ANA? — It reduces flares, is safe long‑term, and does not increase infection risk like high‑dose steroids.

A patient on hydralazine develops arthralgia and a positive ANA. How do you differentiate drug‑induced lupus from idiopathic SLE? — Drug‑induced lupus usually has antihistone antibodies, lacks renal or CNS involvement, and improves after stopping the drug.
In a setting without IIF, how would you screen for ANA? — Use ELISA panels for common nuclear antigens, but interpret cautiously as sensitivity is lower.
What red‑flag sign in a lupus patient mandates immediate referral? — New onset proteinuria >0.5 g/day or rising creatinine indicating possible lupus nephritis.

How does ANA testing help differentiate mixed connective tissue disease from systemic sclerosis? — MCTD shows a speckled pattern with high anti‑RNP; systemic sclerosis often shows nucleolar or centromere patterns.
A patient with suspected vasculitis has a negative ANA but positive ANCA. Why is this important? — ANCA points toward small‑vessel vasculitis (e.g., GPA) rather than a ANA‑associated disease.
